title: Jude and the Visitor
premise: Folklorist Noor Lockridge has spent a decade in the village of Hollowmere, documenting songs the locals refuse to sing twice, while telling themselves the nightly sounds from the old well are settling pipes or wind. When an excavation crew unearths a door sealed from the inside, the village's careful invisibility shatters, and Noor learns the song they've been transcribing is a covenant: the last verse was never sung, only survived, by whoever shut the door. As the well begins to refill and the thing behind the door learns Noor's name, they must recover the final verse from the village's last keeper—without ever singing along—because the song only ends for those who refuse to join it. In the end, Noor sings nothing, holds the verse in silence as the door closes a second time, and chooses to stay in Hollowmere not as an observer but as the next keeper, paying the price of belonging.
about_author: M. M. Nystrom is the pen name of a former field archivist who spent years collecting oral histories in remote coastal and moorland communities, an experience that left a lasting unease about what people choose not to record. Nystrom now writes horror from a house with too many doors, insisting the extra one was on the survey.

chapters.title: The Song Nobody Sings Twice
chapters.summary: Noor Lockridge's POV. Noor records an elderly singer, Edith Marr, who stops mid-verse and refuses to continue, then burns the tea she was pouring without noticing. The village watches Noor with a politeness that feels like a held breath. Emotional beat: the reader feels Noor's decade of rationalism beginning to strain.

chapters.title: Settling Pipes
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, night. Noor catalogs the well's sounds—scraping, a wet rhythm, something almost like humming—and writes three explanations in a journal, crossing none of them out. A neighbor, Tam, warns them off the common after dark with a smile that doesn't reach his eyes. Emotional beat: dread disguised as routine.

chapters.title: Groundwork
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. An outside excavation crew arrives to survey the collapsed chapel grounds, hired by absentee landowners; the villagers react with coordinated, eerie calm. Noor, thrilled by the disruption, agrees to help document the dig. Edith tells Noor: 'They came for the door, not the stones.' Emotional beat: complicity—Noor invites the disaster.

chapters.title: What the Well Remembers
chapters.summary: Noor's POV with a brief Edith interlude. Noor plays back ten years of field recordings and realizes the well's sounds have been answering the songs—each refrain followed, seconds later, by a deeper version from below. Emotional beat: the rationalist's ledger finally tips.

chapters.title: The Door Sealed from the Inside
chapters.summary: Crew foreman Dara Osei's POV. The crew breaks through the chapel crypt and finds a stone door with no handle, its bolts driven from within, and a ring of candle wax older than the chapel. Dara orders it photographed, not opened. That night, the well goes silent for the first time in Noor's recordings. Emotional beat: the held breath releases.

chapters.title: Invisible Was Never an Option
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The village turns on the crew—quietly, totally; supplies vanish, trucks won't start, and the landowner's calls go unanswered. Tam tells Noor the truth in pieces: Hollowmere exists to keep the door shut, and every household owes a verse. Emotional beat: Noor realizes they were never a guest, only unbilled.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Ledger
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith reveals the ledger: names, dates, and a column of verses, each household assigned one line of the sealing song, sung nightly at the well since before records. Her own line is the penultimate verse. The last verse has no name beside it. Emotional beat: grief for a lifetime of unpaid duty.

chapters.title: Refill
chapters.summary: Dara's POV. The well begins to rise, black water climbing past levels marked in centuries-old notches. The crew's youngest member, Pell, sleepwalks to the wellhead and has to be dragged back, humming a tune no one taught him. Emotional beat: the countdown becomes physical.

chapters.title: Verse by Verse
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor transcribes the covenant song from Edith and the ledger, learning its structure: each verse is a lock, and the song must be sung whole, in order, by the named. Noor asks who sings the last verse. Edith: 'Whoever's left.' Emotional beat: the shape of the trap becomes visible.

chapters.title: The Humming Well
chapters.summary: Dara's POV. The well's hum resolves into the covenant song, sung slightly wrong, like something learning it. Pell is found at the crypt door, fingertips bleeding, tracing the bolts. Dara seals the crew in the farmhouse and sends a radio call that returns as their own voice, a half-second late. Emotional beat: isolation closes in.

chapters.title: What Noor Owes
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor searches their own decade of recordings and finds their voice, captured in ambient takes, already woven into the well's humming. They have been singing along for years without knowing. Emotional beat: horror of identity—the observer was always a participant.

chapters.title: The Night of the Open Door
chapters.summary: Dara's POV. The bolts withdraw on their own. The crew flees; Pell is lost to the crypt, and what comes back up the well-shaft wearing his voice asks Dara, politely, for the rest of the song. Dara runs to Hollowmere. Emotional beat: full breach; the price of survival becomes literal.

chapters.title: Edith's Verse
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith sings her penultimate verse at the wellhead as the water rises, and it holds—for a night. She collapses afterward, her voice gone, and passes the ledger to Noor with her own name inked beside the final verse. Emotional beat: succession as both honor and sentence.

chapters.title: The Village That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor walks Hollowmere and finds houses empty, doors open, meals warm—every villager gone between one bell and the next, absorbed as verses. Only Tam remains, and he doesn't remember his own name until Noor reads it from the ledger. Emotional beat: belonging revealed as consumption.

chapters.title: Learning Without Singing
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor memorizes the final verse—silent, mouthing nothing, writing it in a cipher of their own design—while the thing in the well rehearses the song in the voices of the vanished. Each rehearsal, the last verse is a blank it cannot fill. Emotional beat: fragile hope built on silence.

chapters.title: Dara's Bargain
chapters.summary: Dara's POV. Dara offers the thing at the well a deal: open the door and leave, and she'll sing the verse herself. Noor refuses—the verse sung by the willing is a key, not a lock. Dara, half-convinced she's already lost, agrees to hold the door line instead. Emotional beat: the temptation of surrender.

chapters.title: The Well at Full Rise
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The water reaches the crypt threshold. The thing speaks in Edith's restored voice, then in Noor's mother's, offering belonging, an end to ten years of watching. Noor nearly answers aloud and stops themselves at the first syllable. Emotional beat: the climax's threshold—identity against appetite.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Climax, rotating Noor/Dara POV. At the wellhead, Dara sings the covenant from the first verse; Noor holds the final verse in absolute silence, mouthing nothing, as the water and the voices surge to complete it through them. Noor's silence is the lock's last tooth. The door slams; the well drains to a thread. Emotional beat: triumph achieved by refusal.

chapters.title: What the Silence Cost
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The village is emptier than before; Dara leaves with the crew's records and a warning never to return. Noor finds Edith's body at the wellhead, peaceful, her ledger column finally complete. Noor buries her and burns nothing. Emotional beat: mourning without catharsis.

chapters.title: The New Keeper
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor writes to the university resigning their fellowship, mails the field recordings minus one tape, and takes Edith's chair by the well. The villagers who remain—Tam and a handful of returned names—begin teaching Noor the verses they still own. Emotional beat: belonging accepted on its terrible terms.

chapters.title: The Song's Last Verse
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor teaches the covenant to themselves nightly, singing every verse but the last, which they keep sealed in memory and cipher. The well hums along, patient, still missing its final line. Emotional beat: vigilance as a way of life.

chapters.title: Recorded for No One
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, epilogue. Years later, a visiting folklorist arrives asking about a song the village refuses to sing twice. Noor welcomes them warmly, pours tea, and begins the interview—listening, as they once did, for the moment the visitor's voice joins the well. Emotional beat: the cycle continues, and Noor has chosen their side of it.
